Construction of the Real Numbers

The hole in the rationals gets filled and a real number is actually built. One real number is defined as a bundle of rational sequences.

Lengthen the decimal expansion and the rational terms march into the hole. Sequences whose difference vanishes count as the same number. That bundle itself is one real number. Built this way, the number line ends up with no holes. Completeness is exactly what this construction buys.

For example, climb a 🪜 staircase one step at a time toward the top. The numbers 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414 are footprints heading upward. The whole parade of footprints is the destination itself: the real number.

Prove that the termwise sum (xn+yn)(x_n + y_n)(xn​+yn​) of two rational Cauchy sequences is again Cauchy.

∣(xm+ym)−(xn+yn)∣≤∣xm−xn∣+∣ym−yn∣|(x_m+y_m)-(x_n+y_n)| \leq |x_m-x_n| + |y_m-y_n|∣(xm​+ym​)−(xn​+yn​)∣≤∣xm​−xn​∣+∣ym​−yn​∣
Show proof

  3. With N=max⁡(N1,N2)N = \max(N_1, N_2)N=max(N1​,N2​), the right-hand side is below ε2+ε2=ε\frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon2ε​+2ε​=ε for m,n≥Nm, n \geq Nm,n≥N.

    So (xn+yn)(x_n + y_n)(xn​+yn​) is Cauchy.

    Changing representatives to (xn′)∼(xn)(x'_n) \sim (x_n)(xn′​)∼(xn​) still gives (xn+yn)−(xn′+yn)=(xn−xn′)→0(x_n+y_n) - (x'_n+y_n) = (x_n - x'_n) \to 0(xn​+yn​)−(xn′​+yn​)=(xn​−xn′​)→0, hence the same class — addition is well-defined, independent of the chosen representatives.
